title: Bubbles
objective: After this level you can explain speculative bubbles, from Dutch tulips to dot-com stocks.
summary: A bubble is a price far above what fundamentals justify, kept up by buyers hoping to sell higher. Tulip mania was smaller than its legend; the dot-com bubble burst in 2000.

cards.headline: In February 1637, the Dutch market for tulip bulbs cracked.
cards.body: It has long been called the first recorded speculative bubble. But what is a bubble, and was this really one? The legend and the archives disagree.

cards.headline: What makes a bubble
cards.body: A bubble is when an asset's price sits far above what its fundamentals justify, and stays there for a long time. Why would anyone overpay? Because they expect to sell to someone even more optimistic. The catch: bubbles are hard to spot while you're inside one, and many are only called bubbles in hindsight.

cards.headline: Tulips: a virus, a crash, a myth
cards.body: Dutch collectors prized "broken" tulips with striped petals. The stripes came from a virus, which made those bulbs rare and unpredictable. In February 1637 the market cracked, as many buyers said they couldn't pay the prices they had agreed. Charles Mackay's 1841 book told of everyone from merchants to chimney sweeps joining in. Historian Anne Goldgar searched the archives: few people were involved, and she couldn't find anybody who went bankrupt.

cards.headline: Dot-com: a bubble with a stock ticker
cards.body: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups, many with little to show in products or profits. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index peaked in March 2000, and by October 2002 it was down more than 78%. Were bubbles like this obvious? Economists still argue. In 2013, the Nobel went to both Robert Shiller, who argues prices can drift far from fundamentals, and Eugene Fama, pioneer of the view that markets are efficient.

cards.headline: Bubbles: popped
learned: A bubble: prices far above what fundamentals justify
Buyers hope to sell to someone more optimistic
Tulip mania cracked in 1637, but was smaller than legend

questions.prompt: What did historian Anne Goldgar find about tulip mania?

options.label: It ruined the whole Dutch economy
options.rationale: That's the legend she tested and rejected.

options.label: Tulips were never sold for money
options.rationale: They were; the market cracked in 1637.

options.label: Few took part, and she found no bankruptcies
A banking collapse caused the crash
options.rationale: The crash came when buyers couldn't pay agreed prices.

questions.explanation: Goldgar found few people involved, minor damage and nobody she could identify as bankrupt.

questions.prompt: In a bubble, why might someone pay more than an asset's fundamentals justify?

options.label: A law sets a minimum price
options.rationale: No law is involved; expectations drive it.

options.label: They expect to sell to someone more optimistic
They can't find out the current price
options.rationale: Prices are public; buyers are betting on higher ones.

options.label: Its fundamentals are rising just as fast
options.rationale: Then the price wouldn't be above what fundamentals justify.

questions.explanation: Buyers in a bubble pay up because they expect to sell to someone even more optimistic later.

questions.prompt: Late-1990s buyers bid up internet start-ups with little profit. From Level 33, which way can a share pay were they counting on?

options.label: Dividends paid out of the company's earnings
options.rationale: Many start-ups had little profit to pay out.

options.label: Interest at a fixed rate
options.rationale: That's how a bond pays, not a share.

options.label: Capital appreciation, a rise in price

questions.explanation: With little profit to share, dot-com buyers were betting on selling higher later: capital appreciation.
